A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NOBLE and retain matching methods and experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original NOBLE training and evaluation on PVALB neuron simulations, comparisons with experimental recordings, interpolation experiments, and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds VIP evaluation, embedding and training-diversity ablations, and feature-specific fine-tuning experiments.

M1.justification: The sinusoidal embeddings and FNO architecture remain intact. v3 adds optional feature-specific fine-tuning using a weighted combination of voltage-trace and feature losses, demonstrated for sag_amplitude in Section 4.6 and Appendix D.7.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates NOBLE on PVALB models; v3 additionally trains and evaluates it on a VIP interneuron in Appendix D.3. VIP already appeared illustratively in v1 Figure 2, but without this NOBLE evaluation. The task remains single-neuron voltage prediction under square-pulse currents.

E2.justification: v3 adds comparison controls within NOBLE: absent, single-feature, and three-feature embeddings in Table 1, and data-only versus feature-weighted fine-tuning in Table 3. The external HoF/PDE references remain unchanged; newly discussed methods such as NeuPRINT are not experimentally benchmarked.

E3.justification: Reported training changes from 37,800 to 75,600 samples, 350 to 300 epochs, and learning rate 0.008 to 0.004. v3 adds protocols for varying HoF diversity at fixed sample count and subthreshold fine-tuning. Experimental feature comparisons switch from spikecount to mean_frequency to accommodate differing stimulus durations.

E4.justification: New Tables 1–3 test embedding necessity and dimensionality, dependence on training-model diversity, and the effect of feature-loss weighting during fine-tuning. These substantially extend the analyses beyond v1's subsampling and interpolation studies, which remain represented.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 7 displays medians and mean ± one standard deviation bands; v3 Figure 5B uses interquartile-range bands. The subsampling analysis retains its mean, standard deviation, and minimum–maximum reporting. Neither version reports repeated-training seeds or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive quantitative results, including 2.5% VIP voltage error, failure to fire without embeddings, and sag_amplitude error falling from 69.6% before fine-tuning to 9.6% with feature weighting. Table 2 newly quantifies errors under reduced HoF diversity. The headline 2.18% PVALB error and 4200× speedup persist; revised settings prevent interpreting the additions as matched-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: v3 formally introduces the feature-error term and weighted composite fine-tuning objective in Section 4.6 and Appendix D.7. The FNO and sinusoidal-embedding mathematics are otherwise retained through relocation and notation changes. No new theorem or proof is added; the relative-Lp formula explains an existing metric.

C1.justification: The central claims about ensemble modeling, latent interpolation, and acceleration remain. v3's contribution statement adds claims that biological embeddings are critical and that feature-specific fine-tuning can improve targeted features while preserving overall dynamics.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly acknowledges that one experimental trace at each of nine amplitudes cannot directly validate trial-to-trial variability. It also explains spike-width metric sensitivity, dependence on sufficient HoF diversity, and solver-overfitting concerns. Appendix F expands applicability qualifications beyond the single-neuron and low-dimensional embedding limitations already stated in v1.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a NOBLE-specific implementation link, reports approximately four days of training and the training hardware, and specifies time-grid and stimulus durations. It also documents VIP and fine-tuning hyperparameters. v1 provides architecture, optimizer, inference-hardware, and library information but lacks these substantial additions.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion of stochastic neuron models and distinguishes NOBLE from NeuPRINT's population calcium-imaging setting. It adds supporting VIP, Patch-seq, and neural-operator references. Much of the earlier electrophysiology literature discussion is retained in Appendix A rather than replaced.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites and reorganizes the introduction and results narrative. Detailed related work, FNO background, timing information, and limitations are consolidated into dedicated appendices, while the main text gains separate embedding-analysis and fine-tuning sections. These changes extend beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: The main result displays are extensively redesigned: v1 Figures 4–7 are reorganized into v3 Figures 3–5, combining experimental, PDE, and NOBLE comparisons and merging ensemble and feature-error panels. v3 adds three tables and supplementary plots, revises axes and legends, and adopts a conference layout.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked controlled evidence for embedding necessity and the required diversity of expensive HoF training models. v3's ablations address these central gaps, while VIP evaluation and implementation access strengthen validation and reproducibility. The duration-aware metric and explicit single-trace limitation improve interpretation. Direct validation of experimental trial-to-trial variability remains unresolved, but the overall evidence and transparency improve substantially.
